doc.title: Håkan Rydin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Glasgow, Scotland, July 27, 2016

title: Parents' support and choosing jazz; first jazz student at Malmö
summary: Parents were supportive; Rydin weighed teaching and other music, studied at university, then became Sweden's first jazz student at the Malmö academy.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Right. Well did your parents support your path as a professional musician?

Yes. I had no problems with that. I had those kind of parents that say what you do is fine. That’s correct. All the time. But to make it a little more complicated, when I was 18, 19, 20, I mean you decide what to do with your life. Of course I had played jazz for so long I wanted to play jazz. But I also realized that if I was going to be a full time jazz musician I had to lead a very special life and travel a lot and have problems with family life and that.

And so I thought about the options of becoming a music teacher, but it didn’t really interest me; classical music — no that wasn’t it; dance music was not it; rock music was not the music. So I wanted to play jazz. And I studied at the university, but other things. So when I studied, I studied for let’s say 45 minutes by the book and then I’d go 45 minutes by the piano. And that was a perfect combination. Because I could do that forever until I was hungry, you know. And I wouldn’t have been a better musician if I’d skipped the university. In the university I did fine. I had good grades, and so it was a pretty good combination. And then after four or five years I got a call from the music academy in Malmö in southwest Sweden where I live, they said, “we are starting a new education.” This was in the mid-70s, pretty early. “We are starting the education of jazz and improvisation. Do you want to take part in that?” And I was, even at that time, an established jazz musician in Sweden. So I was the first jazz student in Sweden. There were four of us and we graduated a couple of years later and after that I got one student at the academy. And a couple of years after that I got two or three or four, and then it went on.
